data.title: Time out! A reality check on business aviation's sustainability record
data.description:
A recent opinion piece in the Hill sought to capitalize on a beloved global event to disparage an essential U.S. industry, business aviation, in connection with this summer’s FIFA World Cup games.

Beyond grandstanding about cherry-picked flights conducted during a 39-day tournament held once every four years, the author’s flawed analysis omitted key facts about business aviation’s sustainability record.

First, experts have long noted that business aviation accounts for a tiny fraction of transportation emissions. Yet even with its minimal carbon footprint, the sector has slashed emissions by 40 percent in just four decades, with breakthroughs including lightweight composites, winglets and satellite-based avionics, among many carbon-cutting technologies.

Looking ahead, we plan to achieve net-zero emissions by focusing on innovations including development of highly efficient aircraft engines, and new, electric, hybrid and even hydrogen-powered propulsion systems, as well as sustainable aviation fuel, which can cut lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by 80 percent.

Earlier this year, the business aviation sector worked with U.S. House leaders to advance legislation that expands biofuels development by the Department of Agriculture to include sustainable aviation fuel. Congressional lawmakers and other federal government leaders understand sustainable aviation fuel offers benefits well beyond aviation. Industry groups also recognize its promise: the Americans for Clean Aviation Fuels Coalition estimates that its domestic production would add over $78 billion to gross domestic product and support more than 400,000 jobs by 2036, creating new business opportunities for farmers and rural communities, and increasing U.S. energy independence.

Perhaps most important is the industry’s economic impact, including on the World Cup matches. Business aviation supports 1.3 million American jobs and $340 billion in economic activity each year; during the FIFA tournament, business aviation activity helped drive an economic surge at local airports, hotels, restaurants and countless other businesses near host city venues.

The business aviation community thanks Congress for recognizing the industry’s importance, and working with the sector to advance innovations in sustainability. It is unfortunate that some come away with such an unbalanced view of an important issue and a key American industry’s leadership on it.

Ed Bolen is President and CEO of the National Business Aviation Association.

data.title: Harris throws support behind El-Sayed in Michigan: 'I proudly stand with him'
data.description:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris endorsed Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, on Friday. 

“Dr. Abdul El-Sayed understands that the power is with the people, and that the stakes couldn’t be higher in this election,” Harris said in a statement. 

“While Michiganders struggle to afford everyday essentials — housing, gas, groceries, health care, and child care — Trump and Republicans in Congress are giving away $1 trillion in tax breaks to the wealthy and powerful,” she continued. “Abdul knows that we need bold solutions to the crises facing America’s working families, and he is ready to take on this fight. I proudly stand with him to ensure we win a Democratic Senate majority in November.” 

Harris is the latest in a string of establishment Democrats to announce their support for the populist candidate. El-Sayed narrowly beat Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the state’s Democratic primary on Tuesday and is set to face former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in November.

El-Sayed praised Harris in a statement released Friday in conjunction with her endorsement. 

“Her support in this race is critical to building an unstoppable coalition against Rogers, Trump, and their assault on our rights and democracy,” the Senate hopeful said. “Just like I stood with her in her effort to defeat Trump, I’m so humbled and grateful for her support in this race to defeat his minion Mike Rogers.” 

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y), who had endorsed Stevens in the primary contest, backed El-Sayed after his victory this week. The populist candidate has said he would vote to replace Schumer as Senate Democratic leader if elected in November. 

In a joint statement with Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Schumer expressed confidence in El-Sayed’s chances against Rogers.

“Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate,” Schumer and Gillibrand wrote. “We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November.”

White House communications director Steven Cheung slammed Harris’s endorsement in a social media post responding to a CNN report about a potential presidential bid from the Democrat in 2028. 

“Kamala Harris, who lost by a landslide, should really re-evaluate her life choices before running for president again,” Cheung wrote in a Friday morning post. 

“She was humiliatingly and embarrassingly defeated, despite the entire media industrial complex backing her,” he continued. “She’s now banking far left by endorsing Communists like Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. What a Dope!”

El-Sayed has rejected labels such as “democratic socialist” and “communist” and has defined himself as a progressive populist.

data.title: Watch live: Senate looks to power through major priorities before August recess
data.description:
The Senate is gearing up for a busy day of votes on Friday as lawmakers try to clear its legislative to-do list before leaving Washington for the August recess.

The chamber is expected to take up a series of nominations, including acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s bid to formally lead the Justice Department. Blanche’s nomination to the full-time position has faced delays amid concerns from some Republicans.

The upper chamber of Congress is also set to consider the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.) Russia sanctions legislation, along with a series of votes tied a continuing resolution to fund the government and the Protect College Sports Act.

Despite pressure from President Trump, notably absent from the slate is the SAVE America Act voter ID bill.

The first set of votes are scheduled to begin at 11:30 a.m. EDT.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: With no definite end in sight on Iran, the president has to either fish or cut bait
data.description:
When you are the president of the United States it is a good idea to play the movie through in your head to the end before you take your country to war. But caution is not President Trump’s style. He is, as Peter Baker put it in the New York Times, “The most impulsive president of modern times,” who “follows his instincts and can completely reverse himself by the day, or sometimes the hour.”

His impulses led him to believe that war with Iran would end quickly, that it would not drag on as his critics alleged.

The war started on Feb. 28. One day later, on March 1, the president said, the war likely would last “four to five weeks.”

On March 5 he said, “The United States military, together with the wonderful Israeli partners, continues to totally demolish the enemy far ahead of schedule and at levels that people have never seen before.”

And two days after that, Trump told reporters on Air Force One that, “We’re winning the war by a lot. We’ve decimated their whole evil empire.”

On March 20 he said, “I think we won. We’ve knocked out their Navy, their Air Force. We’ve knocked out their anti-aircraft. We’ve knocked out everything.”

But it is August, the war still isn’t over. Talks are stalled, and Americans have grown more and more weary of the president’s optimism.

A new Associated Press poll tells us that about two-thirds of all Americans — 64 percent — say the war is not worth fighting. Eighty-seven percent of Democrats are against the war — but so are more than one-third of Republicans — 37 percent.

“The results are a stark repudiation of the Republican president’s approach to the conflict, which has dragged on far longer than he originally predicted,” as the AP explained it.

A spate of new polls don’t look good for the president. He has the support of just 34 percent of Americans in CNN’s latest poll, matching his lowest point just after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. In a new AP-NORC poll, the president’s approval stands at just 33, tying his lowest since 2017. And he has a 32 percent approval rating in a Quinnipiac poll.

But none of that that has stopped him from declaring on Truth Social that, “MY REAL POLL NUMBERS ARE THE HIGHEST THEY HAVE EVER BEEN.”

Putting it all in capital letters, shouting it to the American people, won’t change reality.

And even if Trump really believes what he is putting out, Republicans running for reelection know the truth. And they’re rightly worried. They’re playing the movie through all the way to November — even if the president isn’t.

Kristen Soltis Anderson, a Republican pollster, told the Times that, “The best thing Republicans have going for them is that the Democratic Party is going through its own issues and does not have a crisp message besides ‘Trump is bad.'” Then she added: “However, if the environment truly stays this grim, that may be enough.”

Forgive the cliche, but Trump, more than five months into a war with no definite end in sight, now has a choice: fish or cut bait.

The American people have had enough of his promises to bomb Iran into submission one day, then stopping the next day and hoping diplomacy will get him out of the war. It’s likely he’s lost credibility in Tehran. But he’s also lost credibility here at home. Whether he’s actually confusing the people in charge in Iran is anyone’s guess. But he’s leaving Americans unsure of what comes next — and what his strategy is, if he actually has a strategy. And it’s why his poll numbers are so low.

If current negotiations fall apart, Trump doesn’t have to bomb Iran back to the Stone Age, as he once promised, but he does have to inflict enough pain so that Iran comes to the table to make the kind of deal the U.S. can accept.

Or … he could just walk away and end it. He can even declare victory, if that makes him happy … but nobody will buy it — even if he shouts it in all capital letters on Truth Social. They will know that it did not end well for Americans — not here at home and not around the world.

Those are his choices. Inflict so much pain to the mullahs in Tehran that they — or whoever’s in charge over there — will make a deal, one that not only opens the Strait of Hormuz but also guarantees — with something resembling certainty — that Iran will not have the ability to make a nuclear weapon. Or the president can throw in the towel and go home.

He needs to pick one. The midterms are right around the corner.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page. Follow him @BernardGoldberg.

data.title: Michigan lifts lettuce warnings as cyclospora cases fall
data.description:
Michigan health officials eased the state’s guidance on lettuce consumption on Thursday amid declining numbers of cyclosporiasis cases. 

State residents are now advised to follow “routine guidance” when consuming produce, following earlier “broad, precautionary recommendations” against the purchase and consumption of bagged salad mixes during the height of the outbreak. 

The state has reported 12,485 cases since June, according to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS). Of these cases, 279 have resulted in hospitalizations and two people have died. 

Cyclosporiasis is typically not deadly, and MDHHS noted that the two deaths were also tied to other preexisting health conditions. Symptoms of the illness include diarrhea, loss of appetite and other stomach-related issues.  

The department said in its guidance update this week that most of the exposures to this parasite occurred in late June and early July and that most of the contaminated produce was “likely no longer available for consumption.”

The cyclospora outbreak has affected U.S. residents across 47 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). As of Tuesday, 10,468 laboratory-confirmed cases have been reported to the CDC since May 1, including 517 hospitalizations and the two deaths in Michigan. 

The public health agency noted that the contraction rate of this parasite is likely much higher, pointing to over 12,255 cases that have not been confirmed through lab testing. Many of these unconfirmed cases have come from Michigan. 

No specific grower has been confirmed as the source of this outbreak. Taylor Farms, a major lettuce supplier that services chains like Taco Bell, voluntarily recalled all of its iceberg lettuce grown in central Mexico on July 17. The company said it made this decision “out of an abundance of caution.” 

Michigan residents are still encouraged to avoid recalled lettuce products, and MDHHS said it will “continue to monitor the situation closely” and update health guidance if necessary. 

“Since the start of this outbreak, MDHHS has remained committed to providing timely, transparent information and clear recommendations to Michigan residents,” the state health department’s chief medical executive, Dr. Natasha Bagdasarian, said in the Thursday update. “As new data has emerged, our guidance has evolved to reflect the best available evidence, helping ensure that prevention recommendations are accurate, actionable and responsive to the changing situation.”

data.title: Appeals court blocks Trump's White House ballroom construction
data.description:
A federal appeals court panel blocked President Trump’s White House ballroom in a 2-1 vote on Friday, saying that work must stop except for below-ground construction, including installations Trump says are needed for security. 

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit panel ruled that Congress retains control over funding for development at the White House and had not authorized Trump’s project. 

The court paused its order for two weeks to allow the Trump administration to seek emergency relief from the Supreme Court.

“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for. Until now,” the majority wrote. 

The panel split along ideological lines. The majority comprised U.S. Circuit Judge Patricia Millett, an appointee of former President Obama, and U.S. Circuit Judge Brad Garcia, an appointee of former President Biden. 

In dissent, U.S. Circuit Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee, said the preservationist group that is challenging Trump in court had no right to sue and the project was likely within the president’s authority. 

“The district court seized supervision of construction at the White House, and my colleagues affirm this judicial overreach,” Rao wrote. “Because the injunction is beyond the proper province of the federal courts, construction should be allowed to continue.” 

Last fall, Trump tore down the East Wing to make way for the new 90,000-square-foot project at the White House. As his administration defends its legality, it has increasingly emphasized a national security need for the ballroom in the wake of recent shootings near the president’s location. 

The D.C. Circuit had allowed construction to continue for months until it issued the ruling.

data.title: The US should invest in light crude refining before the next chokepoint closes
data.description:
During the Cold War, the U.S. was vulnerable to supply shocks, such as cuts to its supply of imported crude oil. In 1979, the Iranian Revolution demonstrated that vulnerability by pushing crude prices from roughly $13 to $34 per barrel within a year. That experience drove successive American administrations to pursue energy independence, a goal they backed with waves of investment in domestic supply and refining infrastructure. 

The shale revolution, in which American companies used hydraulic fracturing after 2008 to unlock new sources of light crude, then made the U.S. the largest oil-producing nation on the planet by 2018. This revolution did not deliver the fuel security its output figures promised. Because the country’s refining infrastructure was built largely around heavy grades, refiners on the Gulf Coast have been unable to capitalize on the light crude flowing out of the shale fields. As a result, the U.S. has had to sell that light crude to its allies in Europe and East Asia. 

America should invest in light crude refining for three reasons: to keep fuel flowing at home when a maritime chokepoint closes, to capture the export margins that foreign refiners now earn on American crude and to gain the diplomatic leverage that comes from supplying allies with finished fuel. 

First, supply resiliency requires refineries built for the light crude that American wells actually produce, since the heavy grades those plants currently run must cross at least one maritime chokepoint to reach the Gulf Coast. 

The Energy Information Administration tracks seven chokepoints, of which the Strait of Hormuz alone carries roughly 20 million barrels per day, about a fifth of world demand. Iran mined the Gulf during the Tanker War of the 1980s, Washington blamed Tehran for limpet mine attacks on six tankers near Hormuz in 2019. Indeed, Houthi missiles have targeted more than 100 merchant ships near the Bab el-Mandeb since late 2023, a campaign that resumed in 2026. 

If any of those closures returned at scale, or if a war over Taiwan shut the Strait of Malacca, American refiners would lose the Saudi and Iraqi heavy barrels they import while domestic light crude sat stranded at export terminals. Because a refinery cannot switch grades overnight, having spent decades tuning its equipment to heavy oil, the mismatch would show up as diesel and jet fuel shortages at home, whichever strait closed first. 

Second, the ability to export refined products would earn American firms more per barrel than the raw crude that goes into them.

In 2023, American refiners shipped out roughly 6 million barrels per day of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products, at margins that at times passed $30 per barrel on diesel alone. When the United States sends its raw light crude to Rotterdam or Ulsan, refiners in Europe and Korea take that margin while American producers collect only the wellhead price. Since the European Union banned Russian diesel in February 2023, European buyers have paid extra for American fuel, a gap that new light crude plants on the Gulf Coast could fill at scale. 

Third, foreign policy leverage goes to the country that sells finished fuel, since a buyer of raw crude can more readily find another seller. Because crude oil trades across dozens of suppliers, a customer who loses American barrels can replace them from Guyana or the North Sea within weeks. In contrast, diesel and jet fuel move through a thinner market, in which refining capacity sets the limit, so a supplier of fuel becomes much harder to replace.

Washington could then extend or withhold fuel guarantees in talks with allies in East Asia, where Japan and Korea bring in nearly all of their crude through sea lanes that China could cut. 

The path runs through expansions at existing plants rather than new refineries since no company has built one with major capacity in the United States since 1977. In 2023, ExxonMobil finished a 250,000 barrel per day expansion of light crude capacity at its Beaumont plant for roughly $2 billion, which puts the cost of 1 to 2 million barrels of new light capacity somewhere between $10 and $20 billion. 

Furthermore, the 2025 reconciliation bill redefined eligible energy infrastructure under Section 1706 to include refining. The Department of Energy can now guarantee loans for exactly these expansions from a $250 billion lending cap. Additionally, the Permitting Council could put each project on its FAST-41 dashboard with a binding federal timetable, while Congress could add a 25 percent investment tax credit modeled on the one that moved TSMC and Intel to build chip plants in Arizona and Ohio. 

Because that leverage builds on the first two gains, a refining sector sized for American light crude would protect fuel supply at home through any chokepoint closure, keep the $30 diesel margin with American firms and give the State Department a tool that raw crude exports cannot offer. 

Alvin Camba, Ph.D., is the lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, where he directs SIGMA, a supply chain intelligence program funded by the U.S. Department of Defense to secure America’s critical material supply chains. He is also a nonresident fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Indo-Pacific Security Strategies in the Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security and a senior research fellow at Associated Universities, Inc.

data.title: AI used to create synthetic virus
data.description:
Scientists have used artificial intelligence (AI) to design complete, functioning viruses with genomes never seen before in nature — a breakthrough that could open new avenues for fighting drug-resistant bacterial infections.

A Stanford University-led research team used generative AI models trained on millions of genomes to design viruses, known as bacteriophage, that can kill bacteria like E. coli, according to a study published Friday in the journal “Science.”

Researchers chemically synthesized and tested nearly 300 of the most promising designs, ultimately producing 16 viable phages capable of infecting bacteria that had evolved resistance to natural bacteriophage.

When E. coli developed natural resistance to the phage used as the template for the experiment, a mixture of the AI-designed phages was able to rapidly overcome that resistance, while a comparable mixture of naturally sourced phages was unable to do so, according to the research.

The study is a major step toward preventing deadly unstoppable pathogens and is the first time researchers have demonstrated the emerging technology’s potential power in this space.

The AI-generated phages were not just copies of viruses already found in nature, according to the authors, who noted the process contained new mutations and divergent genes.

But the ability to use AI to design entire functional viral genomes could raise biosecurity concerns and bring additional complications to the federal government’s efforts to oversee high-risk biological research.

The Trump administration issued a policy in June to regulate high-risk life sciences research, including experiments that could make harmful biological agents more dangerous. 

Experts have warned about the security implications of the technology, as AI could increasingly allow researchers to design entire biological systems rather than simply modifying ones that already exist.

data.title: Live updates: Cassidy will back Blanche's nomination, easing confirmation path
data.description:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said Friday morning in a Senate floor speech that he will support acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, likely allowing his nomination to pass the Senate. Cassidy was the final holdout on the nomination.

As the lame duck senator announced his decision, he hesitated, noting he would catch criticism for his decision but assuring his Louisiana constituents that he had thoughtfully considered the vote.

The Senate is scrambling to leave for its August recess but has several hurdles to jump before it gets there after a week of infighting.

The biggest items on the list include Blanche’s nomination for the permanent job and a continuing resolution to fund the government into December.

Starting with a morning vote series, the upper chamber will try to pass a Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and a bloc of nominees. It will also vote on college sports legislation.

President Trump on Friday has policy meetings at the White House and a roundtable at the State Department, before heading to Bedminster, N.J.

Follow live here.

data.title: Cassidy will support Blanche, sealing confirmation to head Justice Department
data.description:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) announced on Friday morning that he will support Todd Blanche’s nomination to serve as attorney general, all but ensuring that the controversial nominee will have the votes he needs to be confirmed.  

“All considered, I will vote for Mr. Blanche,” Cassidy announced.

Cassidy was the last Republican senator to remain undecided on Blanche, keeping his colleagues in suspense for days about how he would vote.

On Friday he revealed that answer to be “yes,” despite concerns he raised in recent weeks about Blanche’s willingness to serve as an effective check on Trump after previously serving as his personal defense attorney.

Cassidy’s support paves the way for Senate Republicans to advance his nomination on Friday or sometime over the weekend after they finish voting on a Russia sanctions bill, a stopgap measure to fund the government and a bipartisan bill to reform the rules for compensating college athletes.

The Louisiana senator announced his “yes” vote after two other centrist Republicans, Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), announced they would oppose Blanche.

Collins and Murkowski voiced serious concerns about his ability to preserve the political independence of the Justice Department.  

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) needed Cassidy’s vote to advance Blanche because Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) remains absent from the Senate because of a serious health issue.

Without McConnell, Thune has an effective majority of only 52 seats.

All 47 members of the Senate Democratic caucus, including centrist Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) are expected to vote against Blanche.

Cassidy said he spoke with Blanche about a half dozen times in recent weeks about his confirmation and aired the concerns he had been harboring.

Specifically, Cassidy said he was concerned about allegations of “lawfare” at the Justice Department, such as an effort to indict former Trump White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, who gave damaging testimony about Trump in 2022 before a House special committee that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.

Cassidy made his announcement on the Senate floor shortly before senators were expected to vote on the controversial nominee, who advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee on a party-line vote Tuesday.  

He and Murkowski met with Blanche in the basement of the Capitol Wednesday to discuss their concerns with his nomination.

Cassidy later huddled with his staff on Thursday to mull his looming decision, telling reporters that he hadn’t yet decided how to vote.

Murkowski announced her opposition to Blanche early Friday morning in a press release, explaining that she did not feel confident that Blanche, Trump’s former personal criminal defense lawyer, would serve as an effective check on the president.

“The politicization—even weaponization—of the Department did not start with this administration but has accelerated during it,” she said in a statement.  

“I take issue with the handling of the release of the Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators,” she said, referring to the Justice Department’s effort to indict Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) for recording a video urging U.S. service members to disobey unlawful orders.

Collins announced her opposition to Blanche on Tuesday.

Collins called Blanche “a capable lawyer,” she said the Department of Justice under his leadership has “become increasingly political.”

She argued that Blanche’s leadership has “further eroded the department’s independence” and noted that he approved the order to shield Trump, his sons and the Trump family business from IRS audits, protections “unavailable to other American taxpayers.”

She also pointed to Blanche’s role in approving the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and his recent pledge to an anti-abortion organization that he would seek to prohibit the mailing of abortion medication to women nationwide.
